claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Elevated hydrostatic pressure should be applied to the melt before and during quenching.
Elevated hydrostatic pressure during cooling will reduce the crystal-nucleation rate.
Elevated hydrostatic pressure during cooling will slow atomic mobility in the alloy.
Reduced nucleation and atomic mobility will minimize the formation and growth of primary crystalline clusters.
Suppressing primary crystalline clusters will allow a larger fraction of the liquid to vitrify.
Elevated pressure increases the activation barrier for crystal nucleation.
Pressure-suppressed diffusion and nucleation will produce a kinetically stabilized amorphous structure.
The pressure-stabilized amorphous structure will resist crystallization during subsequent moderate thermal excursions.
Relative to ambient-pressure processing, high-pressure cooling will produce a higher amorphous fraction.
Relative to ambient-pressure processing, high-pressure cooling will shift crystallization onset during reheating to a higher temperature.
Relative to ambient-pressure processing, high-pressure cooling will reduce the extent of primary crystallization.
Under ambient-pressure processing, primary non-eutectic phases form extensively despite rapid cooling.
The amorphous phase produced under ambient-pressure processing has limited thermal stability during reheating.
The intervention is expected to remain effective at cooling rates that are insufficient for complete glass formation and ordinarily permit primary crystallization.
The intervention is expected to remain effective only for reheating protocols that do not exceed an unspecified pressure-stabilized thermal window.
The optimal pressure, cooling-rate boundaries, and reheating conditions remain undetermined.
